title: Crown, defence far apart on sentencing for London police officer convicted in-custody death
subtitle: Crown and defence concede they're far apart on the sentencing of London Const. Nicholas Doering.
article: The Crown and defence concede they're far apart for the sentencing of a London police officer who was convicted of criminal negligence in the custody death of an Indigenous woman more than three years ago.

Defence lawyer Lucas O'Hara argued on Friday that Const. Nicholas Doering should receive three year's probation as part of a suspended sentence after being found guilty of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life in the Sept. 7, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn.

But Crown attorney Jason Nicol asked for a sentence of 20 to 30 months, arguing Doering showed "callous indifference" to Chrisjohn and lied to fellow officers about her deteriorating medical condition.
"The jail sentence should not be crushing, but . . . the message must be sent to society that human life is precious regardless whether you're a drug user," Nicol said.
O'Hara maintained that if there is a jail sentence - something that would cost Doering his job - then it should be in the range of 90 days and served on weekends.
Superior Court Justice Renee Pomerance will hand down her decision March 16.
The day started with victim impact statements from Chrisjohn's family, many of whom filled the 14th-floor courtroom.

The mother of 11 was described as a loving matriarch whose struggles with addiction didn't stop her from providing her family with affection, a sense of belonging and a connection to their Indigenous ancestry.
"The cruelty of her death overwhelms the kindness and gentleness of her soul and for that I am angry," sister Cindy Chrisjohn said in her statement.

Doering, 30, had arrested Chrisjohn, 39, after she was found trying to get into vehicles near Highbury Avenue and Trafalgar Street while high on crystal meth. Three paramedics arrived, but none assessed Chrisjohn, court heard.

London police had arrested Chrisjohn the previous day, when she was also under the influence of crystal meth, but left her at hospital after Ontario Provincial Police, who had an outstanding warrant for her arrest, declined to pick her up until she was cleared medically, court heard.

After the second arrest, Doering drove Chrisjohn to a south-end parking lot and turned her over to two Elgin OPP officers, falsely claiming she'd been in the same unresponsive state since he picked her up, but had been medically cleared.

Doering testified he couldn't remember whether he'd spoken to Chrisjohn during the drive, but he did see her slide down the seat three times and stopped at one point to make sure she hadn't slipped out of her handcuffs.

St. Thomas paramedics were called to the Elgin OPP detachment, where they found a motionless Chrisjohn lying on the floor of her cell, breathing irregularly. She later died at the hospital from cardiac arrest connected to crystal meth use, the court heard.
Doering addressed the court on Friday, giving a tearful apology to Chrisjohn's family.

"I've realized that there's nothing that I can do or say to go back to change the events. But what I can do is that I can tell you that there's not a day that's gone by that I have not thought about Debra and wished that she was still here today," he said.
"If I was able to take your pain and suffering away, I would in an instant."
O'Hara said his client, who is engaged, has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and panic disorder and has suffered shame and humiliation.
"This is somebody who had status in the community," O'Hara said, noting Doering would have to be held in protective custody if he's jailed.
But Cindy Chrisjohn rejected Doering's apology.
"I'm sorry, but I don't believe that," she said outside the courthouse. "His statement was so short."
